Learning notes: The Dollar Index (DXY) — Reading Currency Context

DXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

Summary

DXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits.

What the basket measures

ICE's US Dollar Index measures the dollar against six currencies: euro (57.6%), Japanese yen (13.6%), British pound (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%) and Swiss franc (3.6%). It is heavily weighted toward the euro and excludes many trading partners. A DXY rise therefore does not imply the same dollar appreciation against every currency.

Translation and company earnings

Dollar appreciation against a company's revenue currencies can reduce the dollar value of unhedged foreign earnings. The overall effect also depends on costs, hedges, pricing and the currencies involved. Federal Reserve research describes translation and export-competitiveness channels; it does not establish a universal conversion from a DXY percentage move to S&P 500 earnings per share.

A currency worksheet

Suppose a fictional company earns EUR 1 million and has no hedge. At $1.10 per euro, translation gives $1.10 million; at $1.00 per euro, it gives $1.00 million. That $100,000 difference is an illustration for one currency and one unchanged earnings amount. It is not an EPS forecast, and a move in DXY alone does not supply those exchange rates.

Commodities and other influences

For a dollar-priced commodity with an unchanged dollar price, a weaker local currency raises the local-currency purchase cost. In actual markets, commodity prices also change with supply, demand, inventories and interest rates. An inverse relationship with the dollar can appear in a selected sample, but it is not a fixed rule for gold or any other commodity.

Dollar borrowing in emerging markets

A borrower with dollar debt and local-currency income can face a larger local-currency debt-service burden when that currency weakens against the dollar. Dollar revenues or hedges can offset some exposure. BIS research studies broader links between dollar strength and financial conditions; effects vary across economies and periods, so DXY is not an automatic equity signal.

Compare indicators rather than choose one

Read DXY alongside relevant bilateral exchange rates, a broader trade-weighted dollar index, interest rates and the asset's own context. For a study exercise, compare the same dated observations over a chosen interval and report where relationships change. A correlation does not show that the dollar caused another asset's move or predict the next trade.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

Key takeaways
DXY's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency.
Earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.
Dollar and commodity relationships vary over time.
Dollar debt exposure depends on the borrower's income currency and hedges.
Check your understanding
Largest DXY weight: Options: Yen; Pound; Euro (~57.6%); Yuan. Correct answer: Euro (~57.6%). Why: The euro has a 57.6% weight in ICE's six-currency basket.
Dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has: Options: No foreign exposure; Unhedged foreign-currency earnings; Only dollar revenue and costs; No earnings. Correct answer: Unhedged foreign-currency earnings. Why: Unchanged foreign-currency earnings translate into fewer dollars if the dollar strengthens against that currency. This is not a universal EPS forecast.
A gold-DXY correlation measured over one period: Options: Guarantees the next price move; Proves dollar moves cause gold moves; May differ in another period; Is always positive. Correct answer: May differ in another period. Why: Correlation depends on the selected sample and does not establish causation or a fixed trading rule.
Which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar? Options: One with matching dollar income and debt; One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income; One with no debt; Every borrower equally. Correct answer: One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income. Why: Currency mismatch can increase the local-currency cost of dollar debt service; hedges or dollar revenues can change that exposure.
Sources
ICE — US Dollar Index Composition (https://www.ice.com/insights/indexation-and-etfs/managing-us-dollar-risk-in-uncertain-times)
Federal Reserve — Dollar Appreciation and Corporate Profits (2015) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/notes/ifdp-notes/2015/how-much-has-dollar-appreciation-affected-us-corporate-profits-20150717.html)
BIS — Exchange Rates and Financial Conditions in EMEs (2023) (https://www.bis.org/publications/bulletin-79-lessons-recent-experiences-exchange-rates-capital-flows-and-financial-conditions-emes)
FRED — Broad Trade-Weighted US Dollar Index (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DTWEXBGS)
Practise this lesson

Use $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because TradeHQ does not execute derivatives contracts. Educational simulation only — not financial advice.

References and related pages

Federal Reserve — Dollar Appreciation and Corporate Profits (2015)
BIS — Exchange Rates and Financial Conditions in EMEs (2023)
FRED — Broad Trade-Weighted US Dollar Index
